episodes.name: Era Kovanxhi
post: I recently had the pleasure of interviewing the CEO of BonDo soup, Ms. Era Kovanxhi. Over the past two years I have worked with Ms. Era on executive function skills research at Cedar Hill Preparatory School. A few months ago, when I mentioned my interest in biotechnology and food science, she introduced me to the klotho protein which she has done deep research on in the past. In this episode, Ms. Era describes how she came upon the klotho protein, a natural body chemical that aids in cell health and controls aging, and is working on a product that aids in the production of this protein for those on the go, elderly, and people affected by illness. Through her extensive research and own experience as a busy college student and individual in the workforce, she needed something quick and easy that could provide her with the nutrients she needed. This is how BonDo soup was born. Through talking to founders, I have realized that many of the best products come out of necessity. She has created nutrient dense soup bits created from healthy, whole, and all natural ingredients that she found in her kitchen.

This fall, I will be working with Ms. Era to conduct research on her soup bits and their relation to klotho production in a two part study. In the fall, we will be conducting wet lab research to measure our findings. Additionally, in the spring, we will be asking for consumer feedback on the product to see how customers respond.

It has been such a pleasure learning from Ms. Era through this process. Hearing about her experience as a founder in the food product development space and my involvement in her product's research and testing serve to help me grow as a learner and someone curious about the food industry. Being at the forefront of the process allows me to learn about food development and the founder mentality firsthand.

Your favorite foodie signing off,
Samyuktha

episodes.name: Dr. Xenia Morin
post: Recently, I had the pleasure of speaking with Dr. Xenia Morin for a TRACE interview. I met Dr. Morin around this time last year during the fall of my senior year of high school through the Rutgers The Food, Agriculture, and Marine Ecosystems (FAME) project. At Rutgers she serves as Clinical Supervisor for Agricultural Science Education at the Rutgers Graduate School of Education. She is a true pioneer of collaborative and welcoming learning environments for students. One thing that changed my perspective during the interview was her multi-faceted approach to learning and skill building. Specifically, she spoke of her intersecting interests and experience in STEM (biochemistry) and the humanities and how they served as a bridge for her teaching and work. She encourages students to explore different fields of study through core courses and pursue what they feel most passionate about. For students interested in pursuing food systems and education, she recommends that they speak to people in the field and remain curious. Ultimately, Dr. Morin urges students to focus on their work, follow what they love, and persevere.
Thank you so much Dr. Morin for your time and the lessons you have imparted to all of the students watching this.

episodes.name: Erin Hysom
post: I had the amazing opportunity to speak with Erin Hysom from the Food Research and Action Center (FRAC) this past week. I met Ms. Hysom last year at an American Dairy Association Northeast conference while we were seated next to each other for a panel discussion. Following that event, she invited me to speak on a panel for FRAC during the fall of my senior year of high school.

During this interview, Ms. Hysom and I delved into the Community Eligibility Provision and how she got involved in food security and food policy. This conversation really highlighted that you can get started from a young age and experiences that might seem small at the time can truly influence your entire journey. Additionally, she mentioned that talking to real people at the ground level, whether it be parents, people in the school system, and students is critical to moving policies forward and making the most informed policy decisions. Thank you so much Ms. Hysom for sharing your insights!

episodes.name: Crystal FitzSimons
post: I just interviewed Crystal FitzSimons, the President of the Food Research and Action Center (FRAC). I was lucky enough to connect with Crystal through Erin Hysom and Jordan Baker at FRAC.

During this interview, Crystal spoke about how she believes in the importance of working to end hunger in the US. She spoke about how her background really shaped the skills she uses today. Her degree in Sociology gave her the critical thinking abilities and helped her understand the different forces that go into social change. Her first experience in community organizing was for a housing rights group while in St. Louis where she learned a lot about communication. After moving to Washington, D.C., she worked on transportation issues and their impact on low income communities, then a child advocacy organization, and then joined FRAC. She truly resonated with FRAC’s mission and has stayed there for 27+ years. Through the years, her different experiences within FRAC really shaped how she leads as President from policy to leadership and teamwork. She spoke about the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) which is currently the largest and most effective anti-hunger program. SNAP has served to lower healthcare costs, support academic achievement, and improve healthy development and growth. With the current government administration, many cuts to SNAP have been made. Such changes include 800K people falling off of the program within the first 6 months of the administration, and a $187 billion SNAP cut (over ten years) last summer which led to millions of people becoming ineligible, time limits being put in, and over 5.7 million people losing access to SNAP within the last year. The Food Insecurity Report was also terminated, which served as the basis for critical food insecurity data on what families and individuals across the country are facing and the effects of policy changes, prior to its elimination. She also spoke on how Free School Meals for All has gained traction and support, with 79% of voters in support of the campaign. Through this conversation, what stood out to me the most was when she spoke about how policy changes that we read about in the news on a daily basis likely took a very long period of work and dedication on the backend by people who genuinely care about the issue. They are working to reduce cuts and bring in new changes that bring people the resources they need in order to survive, live, learn, and grow.
Thank you so much for your insights, Crystal.
